title: The Great Disruption: How Machine Intelligence Will Transform the Role of Lawyers in the Delivery of Legal Services
author: John O. McGinnis · Russell G. Pearce

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source shifts attention from the cluster’s central concern—verification risk and weak remedies for direct users—to market disruption, lower prices and the likely failure of unauthorized-practice barriers. It supports expanded AI delivery but does not substantively engage the cluster’s calibrated, risk-sensitive model for access to justice.
qs: While we agree with commentators’ skepticism of the unauthorized practice statutes and concede that those statutes pose some limited risk to the expansion of machine intelligence, we believe they will ultimately fail to stop the progress of machine intelligence in legal services.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source partly shares the cluster’s concern with quality and lower-cost service delivery, and it distinguishes routine-task substitution from roles likely to persist. However, its principal framing is predictive and market-oriented: machine intelligence will substitute for substantial legal labour and erode lawyers’ monopoly despite regulatory barriers. It does not develop the cluster’s central emphasis on multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification or task-specific evaluation.
qs: REGULATORY BARRIERS WILL NOT PREVENT MACHINE INTELLIGENCE             FROM UNDERMINING LAWYERS’ MONOPOLY    Part II builds on the foundation described in Part I: machine intelligence will play an increasing role in the legal services market to the extent that it provides quality, lower cost legal services, or inputs into lawyers’ services.

More generally, we agree that big data is currently an imperfect tool, but like many other sophisticated, imperfect tools, it can substitute for substantial amounts of human labor, and some of the labor will be that of lawyers.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source agrees that machine intelligence first transforms discrete legal tasks, remains uneven across practice areas, and preserves roles for human assessment, advocacy, specialised judgment and client relationships. However, it goes materially beyond the cluster’s cautious, supervised-workflow framing by predicting inevitable machine outperformance on most legal services and substantial substitution for routine lawyers and associates, while giving little attention to verification burdens or apprenticeship risks.
qs: But journeymen lawyers—such as those who write routine wills, vet house closings, write standard contracts, and review documents—face a much bleaker future, because machines will do many such routine legal tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster on task-specific disruption, uneven capability, human–machine combination, oversight and organisational adaptation. However, it goes materially beyond the cluster’s cautious near-term account by predicting accelerating substitution for core legal skills and ultimately the erosion of lawyers’ monopoly, relying substantially on forecasts rather than demonstrated general competence or realised organisational value.
qs: More generally, we agree that big data is currently an imperfect tool, but like many other sophisticated, imperfect tools, it can substitute for substantial amounts of human labor, and some of the labor will be that of lawyers.
Even if the machine intelligence provides very good services, mixing in human intelligence may assure the best possible result.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that personalized legal automation implicates protection boundaries and unauthorized-practice restrictions. It takes a comparatively categorical position—treating tailored assistance delivered by nonlawyers as UPL—rather than addressing the cluster’s broader access-to-justice trade-offs or competing reform proposals.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source accepts that predictive systems provide probabilistic rather than guaranteed answers and that human judgment can remain valuable, especially where data are sparse or law changes. It nevertheless forecasts that comparatively better predictions will substitute for some routine lawyer work, a stronger labour-market prediction that does not negate the cluster’s core distinction between classification or forecasting and sound legal advice.
qs: Predictive analytics will be imperfect, providing likelihoods rather than certainties.
A lawyer’s judgment may still add some value to the predictions derived from machine intelligence, even if the machine prediction alone is better than the lawyer’s prediction alone.

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
st.an: The source supports predictive coding as an institutionally accepted automation that can reduce reliance on manual review while remaining subject to legal and procedural constraints. Its rapid-adoption and efficiency claims are predictions rather than universal performance evidence, and its recognition of unresolved proportionality questions is consistent with the cluster’s case-specific, non-blanket approval.
qs: As a result, some courts have approved predictive coding as a tool of discovery that essentially will make the final decisions of relevance, because they believe the price and performance of e-discovery is at least equal to that of the traditional kind.26 The U.S.

That is not to say that e-discovery will not raise important legal questions of its own, particularly at the beginning of its adoption, such as how it will affect the proportionality principle in discovery.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core supervised-aid framing: machine intelligence is an input that lawyers may adopt while retaining professional control, supervision and responsibility for compatibility with ethical obligations. It does not materially develop the cluster’s later concerns about substantive verification consuming efficiency gains or lifecycle confidentiality controls.
qs: purchasing and deploying machine intelligence as an input, even from an outside consultant, lawyers do not share fees and do not surrender their control of the delivery of legal services.

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: The source supports TAR as an early, practically accepted form of legal automation that retains lawyer input and remains imperfect. Its broader predictions of falling costs, wider adoption and exponential improvement are more speculative than the cluster’s process-specific, governance-focused conclusions, but do not displace its core position.
qs: In predictive coding, lawyers look at a sample of the larger set of documents.
Computer technicians help construct algorithms that predict whether a document is relevant.25 Of course, predictive coding is imperfect, because it can miss some documents.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broad proposition that machine intelligence will commoditize some legal services, enable new entrants and produce uneven competitive effects, while leaving some judgment- or advocacy-intensive functions comparatively protected. Its contribution is predictive economic reasoning rather than empirical evidence, and it does not directly address corporate workflow allocation, pricing reform, junior training or verification.
qs: They will commoditize legal services, permitting clients to make easier price comparisons.
They will also bring in new entrants, both as direct suppliers of services and low-cost providers of inputs to services of lawyers.

kp.k: Machine intelligence threatens lawyers’ market power
kp.d: The authors’ central prediction is that machine intelligence will weaken lawyers’ control over legal services by commoditizing work, enabling price comparisons, and introducing competitors supplying either services directly or inputs to lawyers. They distinguish this disruption from earlier office technologies because machines increasingly substitute for core legal skills and continue improving after becoming competitive with humans. These are prospective arguments published in 2014, not findings about subsequent developments.
qs: Here, we focus on one important consequence: the weakening of lawyers’ market power over providing legal services.
They will commoditize legal services, permitting clients to make easier price comparisons.
They will also bring in new entrants, both as direct suppliers of services and low-cost providers of inputs to services of lawyers.
First, the technology is now beginning to substitute for core legal skills, unlike copying and transcription.

kp.k: Exponential technological growth underpins the disruption forecast
kp.d: The authors ground their projections in improving hardware, software algorithms, connectivity and data availability. They cite a 2011 study reporting computing capacity growth of approximately 58 percent annually, telecommunications capacity growth of 28 percent, and storage growth of 23 percent. Watson’s 2011 Jeopardy victory and applications in medicine serve as cross-domain indications of capabilities relevant to legal work, rather than direct demonstrations of legal performance. They acknowledge uncertainty about how long Moore’s Law will persist but anticipate continued rapid growth through other technologies.
qs: We generally think in linear terms.
But when we understand its power, exponential growth should command our attention.
To be sure, the question remains of how long Moore’s Law will continue.

Second, because increases in the power of computing are exponential rather than linear, computers may be able to undertake complicated legal tasks relatively sooner than it initially took computers to do simpler legal tasks.

kp.k: Predictive coding already changes discovery work
kp.d: Discovery is presented as the most advanced application: lawyers review a sample and technicians help construct algorithms predicting document relevance. The authors acknowledge imperfect retrieval but compare it with human fatigue, boredom and error. They cite judicial approval, including Moore v. Publicis Groupe, and occasional Department of Justice antitrust approval as evidence of acceptance. Large firms’ internal discovery units and independent providers illustrate changing delivery arrangements. From their 2014 vantage point, they predict predictive coding in essentially all large-scale litigation within a decade.
qs: Predictive coding has fundamentally transformed the prospects for e-discovery.
In predictive coding, lawyers look at a sample of the larger set of documents.
Of course, predictive coding is imperfect, because it can miss some documents.
The timeline for law firms to adopt e-discovery is likely to be quite quick, with firms using some form of predictive coding in essentially all large-scale litigation within the next decade.

kp.k: Legal research could progress toward automated issue spotting
kp.d: The authors distinguish existing computerized research from projected semantic search that recognizes concepts, evaluates precedential strength and guides precedent selection. They cite network analysis and startups structuring cases or connecting briefs to outcomes as early developments. They forecast a first phase of mature semantic search and evaluation of precedent within ten to fifteen years of publication, followed by a second phase in which systems identify issues from facts. They qualify the timing as dependent on improvements in the larger general-search market.
qs: But machine intelligence will also make judgments about the strength of precedent.
Network analysis can now evaluate the strength of a precedent by considering how much other cases rely on it.
In the second phase, the search engine itself will identify the issues implicated within a given set of facts and then suggest the case law likely to be on point for the issues it identified.
We expect that the first phase of perfecting semantic search, including the evaluation of the strengths and uses of precedent, will come in the next ten to fifteen years.

kp.k: Document automation reduces drafting inputs before replacing oversight
kp.d: Existing personalized forms from LegalZoom and other providers underpin the authors’ forecast that computer-based services will routinely produce first drafts of most transactional documents within ten to fifteen years. As an example of savings, they report Fenwick & West technology officer Matt Kesner’s account that startup incorporation drafting fell from about 20 to 40 billable hours to a handful of hours. They retain substantial lawyer editing in the initial stage and speculate that linking contracts with subsequent court decisions will enable continual improvement.
qs: Of course, at first, lawyers will still be very involved in marking up the first drafts that machines create.
But even at this stage, the savings can be very large.
We predict that within ten to fifteen years, computer-based services will routinely generate the first draft of most transactional documents.

kp.k: Automated briefs are forecast from journalism analogies
kp.d: The authors use the Los Angeles Times’ earthquake-reporting software and Narrative Science’s business and sports stories as analogies for future legal writing. They predict initially rough briefs and memoranda requiring substantial rewriting, comparable to drafts prepared by associates or research assistants. Linking writing systems with legal research is expected to produce useful drafts within fifteen years, with more finished outputs potentially emerging in the following decade or two for low-value transactions. This is explicitly a forecast rather than evidence of mature automated brief writing in 2014.
qs: At first these documents will serve as very rough drafts and will require very substantial additions and rewriting.
As with legal search, we expect substantial progress in programs over the next fifteen years until they deliver very useful drafts.
In the decade or two after that, such programs may deliver more finished products, at least for low-value transactions.

kp.k: Predictive analytics could displace some lawyer assessments
kp.d: The article contrasts lawyers’ experience-based intuitions with systematic analysis of larger datasets. It reports a Supreme Court forecasting model that outperformed a set of experts and Lex Machina’s use of historical patent-litigation data. The authors expect similar approaches in other fields within a decade, while acknowledging that patent litigation is relatively self-contained and economically attractive. Predictions remain probabilistic, and combining lawyer judgment with machine predictions may still add value. They also acknowledge that small samples and rapidly changing law limit analytics.
qs: But their advice is based on their intuitions and limited to their direct or indirect experience of law.
Predictive analytics will be imperfect, providing likelihoods rather than certainties.
But predictive analytics can still displace some lawyers by making better predictions than they do.
A lawyer’s judgment may still add some value to the predictions derived from machine intelligence, even if the machine prediction alone is better than the lawyer’s prediction alone.

kp.k: Better forecasts could encourage settlement and reduce trials
kp.d: The authors predict that improved estimates of case value will bring parties’ assessments closer together and accelerate settlement. Legal fees create a settlement window even without identical valuations, while risk aversion makes certainty attractive to some parties. This mechanism could reduce trials and discovery, indirectly affecting oral advocates even if machines do not themselves appear in court. The article presents this as a theoretical consequence of improved prediction, not a measured reduction in litigation.
qs: The rise of legal analytics will also have an effect on the number of cases that go to trial and the amount of discovery.
As legal analytics provide better estimates of a case’s value, parties will converge more rapidly toward an agreement that falls within the settlement window created by legal fees and risk aversion.
With more accurate predictions of case outcomes, fewer trials should occur because more parties will settle.

kp.k: Routine lawyers face pressure while superstars may gain
kp.d: The authors predict declining prospects for nonspecialized lawyers performing routine wills, closings, contracts and document review. Better performance metrics and wider technological distribution could increase returns to exceptional lawyers, particularly where small outcome improvements justify premium services. Partners may substitute machines for associates, lowering staffing costs; although the article calls this greater leverage, it does not report an increase in the non-partner-to-partner staffing ratio. The resulting compensation distribution could become more bimodal, with fewer highly paid winners.
qs: Partners may also be able to substitute machines for associates, thereby gaining more leverage at lower cost.
Accordingly, we may see an even more bimodal distribution of legal salaries, perhaps with a smaller group of even more highly compensated lawyers.
The overall effect of the machine invasion thus will be quite mixed for lawyers, but particularly difficult for nonspecialized lawyers of average or worse than average ability.

kp.k: Novel law and client relationships preserve human roles
kp.d: The authors identify oral advocacy, rapidly changing specialized law and relationship-based counseling as relatively protected activities. Pattern-based systems have less useful data when legal regimes are new or information is highly specialized. Lawyers also establish trust that can help clients recognize long-term interests despite emotional resistance. These protections are qualified: advocacy still depends on research, discovery and documents that the authors expect machines to transform, and better forecasts could reduce disputes.
qs: Lawyers are more likely to excel if they are specialists in novel laws and regulations.
But if the current time is radically disconnected from the past or involves small amounts of specialized information, machines will have less data to analyze.
Machines are unlikely to perform this bonding function and, thus, will be unlikely to substantially affect this important aspect of the lawyer-client relationship.

kp.k: Lower costs could expand access to legal help
kp.d: The authors predict that lawyers who reorganize around machine inputs can serve previously unmet needs among low- and middle-income people and small businesses. Examples include small-business counseling and prenuptial agreements. Automated forms could reduce delivery costs and make services affordable to a larger population. This is an anticipated access-to-justice benefit and business opportunity, rather than a demonstrated reduction in unmet legal need.
qs: Unmet legal needs exist across the nation, generally for low- and middle-income people who cannot afford the prices lawyers charge.
Lawyers can use machines to help generate relevant forms, thereby reducing the costs of providing services and making the services more broadly affordable.
It is especially good for the underserved middle class and even the poor who are more likely to access legal services at prices they can afford.

kp.k: Existing markets provide evidence of commercial traction
kp.d: The article reports legal-search revenue of $8 billion annually around 2010 and global discovery revenue of $3.6 billion in 2010, divided into $1.1 billion in software and $2.5 billion in services; $9.9 billion by 2017 was an external forecast, not an observed result. It reports LegalZoom reaching 2 million customers through 2011, including half a million in 2011, and revenue of $103 million in 2009, $120 million in 2010 and $156 million in 2011. Contract management was described as a $400 million industry in 2013, with experts anticipating 10 to 20 percent annual growth. The authors treat these broad software and service markets as evidence of machine intelligence’s existing competitive significance.
qs: The three areas that have proven most profitable are legal research, discovery, and document generation.
LegalZoom appears to be the industry leader with 2 million customers in its first ten years through 2011, and half a million in 2011 alone.
Accordingly, in these three areas alone, machine intelligence has made significant progress in undermining lawyers’ monopoly.

kp.k: Professional rules accommodate machine inputs under lawyer responsibility
kp.d: The authors interpret the ABA’s 2012 Model Rule amendments as facilitating technological adoption: Comment 8 to Rule 1.1 addresses technology’s benefits and risks, while Rule 5.3 comments permit outside nonlawyer assistance subject to reasonable efforts to preserve professional obligations. They describe machine intelligence as a tool or nonlawyer assistance rather than an impermissible replacement of lawyer control. They also note that responsibility for monitoring a client-selected provider can be allocated between lawyer and client. These are claims about ABA Model Rules and comments, not a finding of uniform state adoption.
qs: To the extent that machine intelligence is an input, lawyers must use it if necessary to provide competent services and should use it if it will help offer excellent services.
In purchasing and deploying machine intelligence as an input, even from an outside consultant, lawyers do not share fees and do not surrender their control of the delivery of legal services.
By permitting lawyers to “share responsibility,” this comment gives lawyers more leeway than the general rule that a lawyer is fully responsible for supervising nonlawyer assistants and vendors.

kp.k: Unauthorized-practice barriers are predicted to remain manageable
kp.d: The authors distinguish lawyer-supervised inputs from nonlawyer businesses directly providing personalized assistance, which they characterize as conflicting with unauthorized-practice laws. Parsons Technology initially faced an injunction over Quicken Family Lawyer, but subsequent Texas legislation permitted such software and the decision was vacated and remanded. Drawing on this history, LegalZoom litigation and commentary by Benjamin Barton, the authors argue that software delivery was becoming de facto deregulated. They acknowledge some inhibition of innovation and greater resistance to combined human-and-software assistance, but predict that consumer demand and internet-based overseas providers will prevent effective exclusion. Their conclusion disputes commentators who expect substantial regulatory obstruction.
qs: Although these laws technically create an obstacle to machine intelligence providing legal services, in practice, the market for these services has become de facto deregulated.
The combined human and computer assistance is the only area where LegalZoom has been forced to significantly alter its business plan.
On the internet, providers based in other countries could readily provide U.S. residents with machine intelligence services providing legal assistance or advice under relevant U.S. law.
Although unauthorized practice of law statutes undoubtedly inhibit innovation to some degree, they present only a manageable obstruction.

kp.k: Human assessment remains despite technological competence concerns
kp.d: The authors report Dana Remus’s concern that lawyers may lack the knowledge to supervise technology vendors or assess whether systems are adequate and working properly. They reject this as a lasting obstacle, arguing that legal experts can assess outputs without fully understanding the machinery and that some experts will retain programming expertise until true artificial intelligence. They also acknowledge big data’s limitations, including correlation rather than causation and weak performance on small samples, while maintaining that imperfect tools can still substitute for substantial lawyer labor.
qs: Another commentator worries that lawyers will not be competent to evaluate machine intelligence.

But as in other areas of technological advance, human legal experts will continue to assess the outputs of machine intelligence, even if as individuals they are unable to understand fully how that machine intelligence works.

More generally, we agree that big data is currently an imperfect tool, but like many other sophisticated, imperfect tools, it can substitute for substantial amounts of human labor, and some of the labor will be that of lawyers.

kp.k: Automation challenges ideological justifications for professional monopoly
kp.d: The authors interpret persistent opposition partly as fear of losing professional monopoly, not simply concern about technological competence. Their theoretical argument identifies inaccessible expertise and lawyers’ public-good orientation as two justifications for professional privilege. If machines supply comparable expertise or make it available to nonlawyers, the first justification weakens. Commodification also exposes the dependence of service quality and legal outcomes on purchasing power, challenging the claim that monopoly promotes equal justice. This is the authors’ explanatory and normative argument, not an empirical finding about opponents’ motives.
qs: We suggest that this opposition derives from two sources: first, fear of machine intelligence and second, fear of the implications for lawyers’ monopoly.
The first element is the belief that legal expertise is inaccessible to nonlawyers.
The second element is the belief that lawyers, in contrast to business people, work to serve the public good.
The commodification of legal services highlights the reality that legal services, and therefore access to justice, are bought and sold.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McGinnis and Pearce predict progressive substitution of machine intelligence for core legal tasks, weakening lawyers’ market power while expanding affordable services.
pts.d: The authors identify five principal areas of change: discovery, legal search, transactional document generation, briefs and memoranda, and prediction of case outcomes. They describe predictive coding as already replacing document-review work and forecast semantic research that evaluates precedent, followed by systems that identify legal issues from facts. They predict increasingly tailored transactional documents and useful machine-generated brief and memo drafts. Predictive analytics will supplement and sometimes displace lawyers’ assessments of litigation prospects; more convergent case valuations should encourage settlement and reduce trials and discovery. At market level, they predict commoditization, easier price and quality comparisons, new entrants, and reduced demand for routine lawyers. They expect particularly successful lawyers to extend their reach through technology, while lawyers using cheaper inputs can serve unmet needs. They argue that professional regulation will not prevent these changes: lawyers can purchase machine inputs within existing ethical frameworks, direct software provision is already substantially deregulated in practice, and overseas internet providers would create further pressure. Their conclusion that machines will ultimately outperform humans in most legal services is a prediction, not a finding from a comprehensive legal-performance test.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supports its forecasts with technological growth studies, existing products and markets, selected empirical research, reported implementation experience, and legal authorities.
pts.d: For the technological trajectory, the authors cite Moore’s Law, Hilbert and López’s 2011 estimates of computing, communications and storage growth, research on algorithmic improvements, and Watson’s Jeopardy performance. These supply the basis for extrapolations rather than direct measurements of future legal capability. For discovery, they cite judicial approval of predictive coding, including Moore v. Publicis Groupe, and Department of Justice acceptance in some merger reviews. For research, they cite existing semantic and structured-search initiatives and research on network-based measurement of precedent. For drafting, they cite LegalZoom, Kiiac, LawDepot and HotDocs, and a reported Fenwick & West implementation that reduced incorporation-document work from roughly 20–40 billable hours to a handful. The Fenwick example is reported practitioner experience, not an independently presented experimental comparison. Automated journalism provides an analogy for future brief writing. For prediction, they cite the Supreme Court Forecasting Project’s model outperforming a group of experts and Lex Machina’s patent-litigation data and services; they do not give an accuracy percentage. Market evidence includes reported legal-search revenue of $8 billion annually around 2010, e-discovery revenue of $3.6 billion in 2010 with a forecast of $9.9 billion by 2017, and customer and revenue growth for document providers. These figures concern the article’s broad category of machine intelligence, including search and automation, rather than contemporary generative AI alone. The regulatory argument draws on the 2012 ABA Model Rule comments concerning technological competence and nonlawyer assistance, the Parsons Technology injunction followed by Texas legislative permission for relevant software, LegalZoom litigation, and commentary on de facto deregulation. ABA Model Rules are discussed as model professional standards, distinct from state unauthorized-practice laws. The authors supply no new comprehensive study establishing their profession-wide employment, earnings, settlement or access-to-justice forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The forecasts are anchored in 2014, with task-specific horizons of approximately ten to fifteen years and more speculative developments beyond that.
pts.d: The authors expect predictive coding in essentially all large-scale litigation within the next decade, approximately by 2024. They forecast semantic research incorporating assessment of precedent within ten to fifteen years, approximately 2024–2029, with subsequent issue spotting left undated. They predict routine first drafts of most transactional documents within the same ten-to-fifteen-year period. Brief and memo programs should produce very useful drafts over the next fifteen years, approximately by 2029; more finished products may follow a decade or two later, especially for low-value transactions. They expect predictive analytics to extend beyond early applications to other practice areas within a decade. These are the authors’ forecasts from 2014, not claims that those milestones have subsequently occurred. Their argument depends on continued improvements in hardware, algorithms, connectivity, data availability and price-performance; legal-search progress particularly depends on broader search technology. They acknowledge uncertainty about the duration of Moore’s Law. Machines are expected to work best in settled, routinized fields with substantial relevant data, and less well in novel, rapidly changing or small-sample fields. Initial drafting requires extensive lawyer revision; outcome predictions remain probabilistic; and human judgment may improve machine predictions. Oral advocacy and relationship-based counseling remain protected for the foreseeable future or at least initially. The authors acknowledge that unauthorized-practice rules can inhibit innovation to some degree, while predicting that they will not stop it.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors anticipate uneven consequences for lawyers but broadly favorable consequences for clients, especially people and small businesses currently unable to afford assistance.
pts.d: Routine practitioners, nonspecialists of average or below-average ability, and junior associates performing review, research and drafting face substitution and downward economic pressure. Partners may replace associate work with machine inputs and lower costs; this describes substitution for human staffing, not evidence that associate-to-partner leverage will rise. Superstars may receive higher rewards as performance becomes more visible and technology broadens their client reach, producing a more polarized earnings distribution. Lawyers reorganizing around inexpensive inputs can expand services for low- and middle-income individuals and small businesses. Court advocates remain necessary but may face fewer trials, while specialists in new laws and fast-changing fields remain valuable because historical data are less informative. Counselors who build trust and persuade clients retain a relationship-based role. Corporate clients and litigants may gain cheaper inputs, improved outcome estimates and more settlement opportunities. Software vendors and independent discovery-service providers gain market opportunities; these are not all the same provider category. The authors predict wider access to justice for underserved consumers, not merely enterprise cost savings. They also argue that machine-delivered expertise challenges both the economic monopoly of lawyers and its ideological justification, including the claim that legal expertise is inaccessible to nonlawyers.
